explainers.title: Hello and welcome to Collaboration
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 5 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. So far, most of your work has been about your own thinking. This unit is different, and rather exciting, because it is about working with other people. The skill is called Collaboration, and it may be one of the most useful skills you ever learn.

Remember the six thinking skills of Global Perspectives. You have already started some of them, and you will keep growing them all:

This whole unit is about the fifth skill: Collaboration. Almost nothing big in the world is built by one person alone. A hospital, a football team, a market, a family meal, a clean schoolyard: all of these need people working together. When you learn to collaborate well, you can do things that would be far too big to do on your own.

Why does collaboration matter beyond school? Think about the grown-ups around you. Builders raising a house in Hargeisa, fishers landing a catch together on the Berbera coast, market traders in Mogadishu, nurses caring for patients, neighbours clearing a street after the rains: they all share a goal, share out the jobs, and sort out any problems together. Across the Horn of Africa, and all around the world, the biggest things are built by teams. A learner who practises collaboration now will be a better teammate, friend, and leader for their whole life. That is why we teach it on purpose.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people to reach a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: So what is collaboration?
explainers.body:
Here is a simple meaning you can keep: collaboration means working together with other people to reach a shared goal. That shared goal has a special name in this unit. We call it a shared outcome: the one result the whole team is working towards.

Good collaboration is really three things joined together, and this unit teaches all three:

Notice that collaboration is not just being in the same room as other people. Five children sitting together, all doing their own thing, are not collaborating. A team is collaborating when they share one outcome, share out the work, and help each other get there. That is the skill you will build.
bullets: Sharing ideas — putting forward your own ideas, and listening carefully to everyone else's.
Planning together — deciding who does what, and how long each job will take.
Solving problems together — finding fair answers to problems and disagreements when they come up.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You might be wondering: how can I learn teamwork when I study at my own pace, on my own? That is a very good question, and the answer is the heart of this unit. You will plan and practise on your own with your AI tutor, and then do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions. Four kinds of support work together:

So the pattern all the way through this unit is simple, and you will see it again and again: plan and practise with your AI tutor now, then carry it out with your group in your next teacher session. In the old style of this subject, a book would say 'talk to your group' or 'discuss as a class'. In our model, you rehearse with your tutor first, so that when you meet your team you are ready to do your best.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and prepare your part in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Your tutor is your planning and rehearsal partner. With it you can plan roles and tasks, practise making and building on suggestions, rehearse resolving a disagreement, and get friendly feedback before you meet your team.
Your teacher sessions, about twice a week. This is where the real collaboration happens. You bring the plans you prepared, and carry them out together with your group of classmates.
Your family and community. The people at home are a real team too. You can practise sharing jobs, listening and encouraging with them any day of the week.

explainers.title: Meet your team for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one group of Year 6 learners all the way through the unit. They are five friends at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa: Layla, Omar, Grace, Malik and Dina. There is no single leader among them. That is the point of a team: everyone matters, and everyone gets a turn to shine.

A clever team knows what each member is good at, so the jobs can be shared out well. Here is what each of them brings:

As you meet each new collaboration skill, you will see exactly what this team does with it. By the end, they will have run a real project together. You will be doing the very same thing, with your own group in your teacher sessions.

headers: A strength they bring to the team
rows: Careful and organised; good at planning the time and keeping the team on track.
Friendly and encouraging; good at talking to people and speaking in front of others.
Good with numbers; enjoys recording answers in neat tables and charts.
Practical; good at making and building things by hand.
Creative; good at drawing, designing, and thinking up new ideas.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: a shared project for the whole team
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. In earlier units your Challenge was mostly yours. This time it belongs to a team, because collaboration only happens when people share a goal.

The team of five chose this Challenge: How can we make sport and play more open to every child at Ehel Academy? They noticed that the same few children played every break, while others, often the girls and the younger ones, watched from the side. Their shared outcome became one clear sentence: *more children, girls and boys, take part in sport and play at our school.*

To reach that outcome, the team has a set of jobs to share out and plan:

You do not have to copy this exact project. Any shared team goal will work: an awareness stall about plastic waste or saving energy, a plan to save water, a tidier schoolyard, or a kinder playground. What matters is that it is a shared outcome your group can reach together.
bullets: Design a questionnaire to find out how much sport children do, and what stops some of them joining in.
Try the questionnaire with a few people, then improve it.
Survey a larger group of children and record the answers.
Plan a fun sports afternoon with easy games that anyone can join.
Make posters and announcements to invite every child.
Give a short presentation about what they found and what they will do.

explainers.title: Three stages of collaboration this year
explainers.body:
Your collaboration skills will grow in three stages, just as they did with research. You will begin by starting each skill, then move on to developing it, and finally you will get better at it. Here is what each stage is really about:

Do not worry if the first tries feel tricky. Starting is meant to feel like a first try. Each skill below will move you a little further along.
bullets: Starting — working with others to solve a problem, and planning teamwork to reach a goal.
Developing — planning a task to reach a shared outcome, introducing useful ideas, and working positively when the team hits a problem.
Getting better — working well on your own tasks that help the team, and planning your team's time so you reach the goal.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Working towards a shared outcome
explainers.body:
Every strong team begins the same way: by agreeing on its shared outcome. A shared outcome is the one result everyone is working towards, written so clearly that every member could say it in a single sentence. Without it, five people can work hard all day and still pull in five different directions.

A good shared outcome is clear (everyone understands it the same way), shared (the whole team wants it, not just one person), and reachable (the team could really get there together).

explainers.title: Skill 2: Making suggestions, and building on other people's suggestions
explainers.body:
Once a team has its shared outcome, it needs ideas. Two skills go together here. The first is making a suggestion: offering your own idea to the team. The second, and often the more powerful, is building on someone else's suggestion: taking their idea and adding to it to make it even better.

Building on ideas is what turns a group of people into a team. Instead of each person fighting for their own idea, the team grows one idea together, and it ends up better than anything one person could have made alone. Helpful starters are: Even better, we could ..., Building on that, what if we ..., and Yes, and we could also ...

explainers.title: Skill 3: Listening to others and encouraging everyone to join in
explainers.body:
A team is only as good as the voices it hears. Some people share ideas easily; others are quieter and need a warm invitation. A strong teammate does two things: they listen properly, and they encourage others to take part, especially the quiet ones.

Listening means letting a person finish, looking at them, and showing you understood, perhaps by saying their idea back: So you mean we could ...? Encouraging means helping someone feel able to speak: Dina, you are good at ideas, what do you think? or That is a good start, tell us more. When everyone is heard, the team gets more and better ideas.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Dividing the tasks fairly, by each person's skill
explainers.body:
A shared outcome usually needs many jobs done. A team that shares these jobs fairly works far better than one where a single person does everything while the rest watch. The clever trick is to divide the tasks by skill: give each job to the person best suited to it, while making sure everyone has a fair share.

Dividing fairly does not mean everyone does the exact same job. It means everyone has a reasonable share that matches their skills, so the whole team feels useful and no one is overloaded.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Making a schedule: who, how long, and when
explainers.body:
Once the jobs are shared out, a team needs a schedule: a plan of who does each task, how long it will take, and when it happens. A good schedule uses two clever ideas that save a lot of time.

Here is the team's schedule for one session preparing the sports afternoon. Notice which tasks run in parallel, and which must wait:

Because tasks 3, 4 and 5 happen in parallel, the whole plan fits into one session, even though the jobs add up to much more than one session if done one after another. That is the power of a good schedule.
bullets: Parallel tasks are jobs that can be done at the same time by different people. While Omar surveys children, Malik can be building the game. Doing tasks in parallel means the team finishes far sooner.

Dependencies are jobs that must wait for another job to finish first. You cannot record the answers until the survey is done, and you cannot make the posters until the date is decided. A dependency has to come earlier in the plan.

rows: 1. Agree the date and which games to play
First of all; every other task depends on this.
At the same time as task 3 (parallel work).
5. Build a bat-and-ball game from spare things
Any time after task 1, in parallel.
6. Put the answers into a table and a chart

explainers.title: Skill 6: Resolving disagreements in a friendly way
explainers.body:
Every team disagrees sometimes, and that is completely normal. A disagreement is not a fight, and it is not a sign of a bad team. In fact, teams that never disagree often miss good ideas. What matters is not whether you disagree, but how you resolve it. To resolve a disagreement means to sort it out fairly, so the team can move on happily.

A friendly way through a disagreement has four steps:
bullets: Listen to each side, letting each person explain their reason without being interrupted.
Find what you agree on. Almost always, both sides want the same shared outcome.
Suggest a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.
Agree and move on, without anyone feeling like the loser.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Problem, action, outcome
explainers.body:
A neat way to plan a team task is a flowchart with three columns: the shared problem you want to solve, the action you will take together, and the shared outcome you hope to reach. Reading it from left to right tells the whole story: this problem, so we do this, to reach this result.

The middle column is the most important, because it is the part the team actually does together. Here are three examples the team mapped out:

Filling in a flowchart like this helps a team see, at a glance, whether their action really joins the problem to the outcome. If the action would not change anything, the team knows to think again.

rows: Lights are left on in empty rooms, wasting energy.
Put friendly reminder signs by the switches, and each class chooses a lights monitor.
Lights are switched off when a room is empty.
Some children never join in sport at break.
Run a sports afternoon with easy games, and invite every child.
More children take part in sport and play.
Plastic bottles are dropped around the schoolyard.
Set out bins for bottles, and each class does a two-minute tidy-up.
The schoolyard stays clear of plastic.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Prioritising: which action should we do first?
explainers.body:
Often a team has more good ideas than time. When you cannot do everything at once, you prioritise: you decide which action is most important to do first. Prioritising well is a real skill, and it keeps a team from wasting its time on something small.

To prioritise fairly, ask a few checking questions about each possible action:

Once you have chosen, be ready to explain why. Useful starters are: The action we are prioritising is ..., then Firstly ..., In addition ..., Furthermore ..., and Finally ...
bullets: Is it about an important problem that really needs action?
Will it actually change what people do, or make a real difference?
Is the outcome realistic in the time and with the help we have?
Will the whole team stay in agreement and be happy doing it?
Do we need help from outside the team, and can we get it?

explainers.title: Skill 9: Introducing useful ideas and working positively
explainers.body:
Two habits make a team a pleasure to be in. The first is introducing useful ideas: not just any idea, but one that really helps the team reach its shared outcome. The second is working positively: staying friendly and hopeful, cheering others on, and looking for what could work rather than only what could go wrong.

When a team plans its actions in detail, a helpful tool is a table with five headings: What?, When?, Where?, Who?, and Why? It turns a vague idea like 'we should save energy' into clear, doable actions. Here is how the team planned to help everyone remember to turn off the lights:

Notice that each action names who does it and why it will help. That is the difference between a wish and a plan. As teammates share ideas for a table like this, they should build on each other positively, exactly as in Skill 2.

rows: Put up friendly reminder signs by the light switches
Dina designs them; Malik puts them up
People forget, and a sign reminds them
Each class picks a lights monitor for the week
One person remembers to check the room
A short talk about saving energy
Omar and Layla give the talk
Everyone hears the message at the same time

explainers.title: Skill 10: Managing your time
explainers.body:
A plan is only useful if the team keeps to it. Time management means noticing how the time is going and making calm choices so the team still reaches its goal. It is not about hurrying or panicking. It is about checking the clock, spotting a problem early, and changing the plan together before it is too late.

Three habits help a team manage time well: check the schedule partway through; if a task runs late, decide together what to move or make smaller; and always keep an eye on the shared outcome, so you spend your minutes on what matters most.

explainers.title: Skill 11: Making an action plan with Red, Amber and Green
explainers.body:
When a project has many steps, a team needs a way to see, at a glance, how it is going. An action plan does this. It breaks the shared outcome into steps and lists, for each one, who is responsible, by when it should be done, what resources are needed, and its status.

The status uses three colours, called RAG for Red, Amber and Green:

The team updates the colours each time they meet, so everyone can see what is done and what still needs attention. Here is part of their action plan for a different goal: saving water at school.

An action plan turns a big goal into small, shared, trackable steps. The colours are honest: a Red step is not a failure, it simply tells the team where to put their energy next.
bullets: Red means the step has not started yet.
Amber means it is started but not finished.
Green means it is complete.

rows: Check which taps drip or are left running
Make please-turn-me-off signs for the taps
Ask the office to mend the dripping tap
Tell every class how to save water
A short talk and a poster

explainers.title: Skill 12: Evaluating yourself and your team
explainers.body:
When a project ends, a strong team does one last, valuable thing: it evaluates. To evaluate means to judge honestly how well things went, so you can do even better next time. You evaluate in two ways: how well you worked as a member, and how well the team worked together.

Evaluate yourself kindly with starters like: A positive contribution I made was ..., One thing I found hard was ..., and Next time I will ... Evaluate the team by asking: did we share the work fairly? Did everyone get to use and grow their skills? Did we reach our shared outcome?

explainers.title: How collaboration helps the other five skills
explainers.body:
Collaboration is not on its own. It makes every other Global Perspectives skill stronger, and they make it stronger too.

So the teamwork you practise now will lift all your other skills. Learning to collaborate well is one of the most useful things you will do this year.
bullets: Research gets easier, because a team can share out the finding-out and gather far more than one person could.
Analysis grows, because teammates see different causes and consequences that you might miss alone.
Evaluation improves, because a team can weigh an idea from many sides before deciding.
Reflection deepens, because you learn about yourself by noticing how you work with others.
Communication matters more than ever, because a team only works if its members share their ideas clearly.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the collaboration cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every collaboration skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one cycle you can use for any team project:
bullets: Agree a clear shared outcome the whole team wants.
Share ideas, making suggestions and building on each other's.
Listen to everyone and encourage the quieter voices.
Divide the tasks fairly, by each person's skill.
Make a schedule: who, how long, and when, using parallel work and dependencies.
Prioritise the most important action if you cannot do everything.
Work positively, and resolve any disagreements in a friendly way.
Track your steps in an action plan with Red, Amber and Green.
Evaluate yourself and your team, and decide how to do even better.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Communication. Once you can work well in a team, communication teaches you to share your ideas and findings clearly, so that others truly understand you. Good collaboration and good communication go hand in hand: a team needs both. Well done for learning to be someone people are glad to have on their team.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a football, and the skill is the game you are learning to play.
In this unit the footballs are real projects: making sport open to every child, an awareness stall about plastic or energy, and a plan to save water.
But the real prize is not the project. It is to become someone people are glad to have on their team.

bigIdeas.title: Two questions every team keeps asking
lines: How well do I work with my team? Do I make useful suggestions, encourage others, and help solve problems?
How well do we work as a team? Do we make a plan, divide the work fairly, and manage our time?
Coming back to these two questions is one of the best ways to become a stronger teammate.

bigIdeas.title: A fair team makes room for everyone
lines: When the team chose the time for the sports afternoon, they checked it worked for every child.
They avoided the middle of Friday, when Muslim families attend prayers, and they did not pick a Sunday morning, when some Christian families attend church.
Planning around what matters to each person is a kind and clever part of collaboration.

bigIdeas.title: What the RAG colours mean
lines: Red: the step has not started yet.
Amber: the step is started but not finished.
Green: the step is complete.
A Red step is not a failure; it just shows the team where to put its energy next.

bigIdeas.title: Your shared project runs through everything
lines: Pick one team project you could really do with your group, such as a sports afternoon, an awareness stall, or a plan to save water.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something your team genuinely cares about.
By the end you will have a real plan your team can carry out.

bigIdeas.title: Parallel work and dependencies
lines: Parallel tasks can be done at the same time by different people, so the team finishes sooner.
A dependency is a task that must wait until another one is finished first.
For each task, ask: can this run at the same time as another, or must it wait for something else?

bigIdeas.title: Four steps to resolve a disagreement
lines: Listen to each side without interrupting.
Find what both sides agree on, usually the same shared outcome.
Suggest a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 5 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Collaboration.
Ask it: in one or two simple sentences, why is being a good teammate useful, even outside of school?
Then tell your tutor about a time you worked well in a team, and a time teamwork was hard, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a team project you could do, real or imagined.
Ask it to help you write your shared outcome as one clear sentence, starting with the words Our shared outcome is.
Then ask: is my shared outcome clear, shared, and something a team could really reach?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one suggestion for your team project, starting with We could.
Ask the tutor to build on your idea, then you build on its idea, back and forth, four times.
Notice how the idea grows. Ask the tutor which version of the idea is strongest, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a time you felt shy to share an idea in a group.
Ask it to give you three friendly sentences you could use to encourage a quiet teammate to speak.
Then practise: the tutor plays a quiet team member, and you gently invite its idea.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the list of tasks for your team project.
Ask it to help you sort them into a schedule with who, how long, and when.
Then ask: which of my tasks could be done in parallel, and which ones depend on another task being finished first?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe a disagreement your team might have to your AI tutor.
Ask the tutor to take the other side, then practise the four steps: listen, find what you agree on, suggest a middle way, agree.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I stay calm, fair, and friendly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor a problem your team wants to solve.
Ask it to help you fill in the three columns: shared problem, action, and shared outcome.
Then ask: does my action really lead from the problem to the outcome, or is something missing?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor three possible actions for your team project.
Ask it to help you weigh each one against the checking questions above.
Then choose one, and practise justifying it: The action we are prioritising is ... Firstly ... In addition ... Finally ...

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one action your team could take for your shared outcome.
Ask it to help you turn the action into a row with What, When, Where, Who, and Why.
Then ask the tutor for one way to say a difficult thing to a teammate positively, without a put-down.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your team's schedule and how much time you have.
Ask it: if one task runs late, which task could we move or make smaller, and why?
Then ask the tutor for one tip to help a team keep an eye on the time without rushing.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a team task you finished, real or from your teacher session.
Ask it to help you evaluate yourself: a positive contribution you made, and one thing to improve.
Then evaluate your team together: did you share the work fairly, use everyone's skills, and reach the goal?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your project and your shared outcome sentence.
Ask it: is my shared outcome clear, and is it something a team of children could really reach?
Ask the tutor to help you make the sentence sharper and simpler.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your first suggestion.
Take turns building on it: the tutor adds an idea, then you add to the tutor's idea, four times in all.
Ask the tutor which version of the idea is strongest, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your list of tasks and skills to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does my way of sharing the jobs look fair, or does anyone have too much?
Ask the tutor if any task needs a skill I have not planned for.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your schedule to your AI tutor.
Ask it: which of my tasks could be done in parallel, to save time?
Ask the tutor which task must be done first, because other tasks depend on it.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three flowchart rows to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does each action really lead from the problem to the outcome?
Ask the tutor to help you improve any row where the action seems too small to reach the outcome.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your three possible actions.
Ask it to help you weigh each one against the checking questions.
Say your justification out loud, and ask the tutor if your reasons are strong and realistic.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your action table to your AI tutor.
Ask it: is any action vague, and how could I make it clearer?
Ask the tutor to check that each action names a person and a reason.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe the disagreement to your AI tutor, and ask it to take the other side.
Practise the four steps out loud, all the way to agreeing a middle way.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I listen, stay calm, and treat the other side fairly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your action plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are my steps in a sensible order, and is anything missing?
Ask the tutor what a team should do about a step that is still Red the day before its deadline.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two stars and a wish to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does my feedback sound kind and encouraging, not like a put-down?
Ask the tutor to help you reword the wish so it feels friendly and helpful.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three team sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: based on what I said, what is one thing I could do to be an even better teammate?
Ask the tutor to help me plan my very next step with my group.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fixed sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrites are now fair, kind, and clear.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to reword any answer you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was strongest, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your teamwork changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor to suggest one collaboration skill to focus on in the next unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A family touch
lines: Ask someone at home about a time they worked in a team, at work or in the community.
Ask them: what made the team work well, and what made it hard?
Bring their answer to your next teacher session. The adults around you are full of teamwork wisdom.

speakingPrompts.title: A family touch
lines: Do a small job with someone at home, such as cooking or tidying, as a team.
Afterwards, give them two stars and a wish, and ask them to do the same for you.

teacherSessions.title: The team agrees its shared outcome
lines: Layla, Omar, Grace, Malik and Dina all cared about sport at Ehel Academy, but at first each imagined something a little different.
So they wrote one shared outcome they could all agree on: more children, girls and boys, take part in sport and play at our school.
Now every job they do points at the same goal. A shared outcome keeps a team pulling in one direction.

teacherSessions.title: The team builds on each other's ideas
lines: Dina says: We could put up posters about a sports afternoon.
Omar builds on it: Even better, let's first ask children which sports they would actually come to.
Grace builds on that: We could make it a short questionnaire, so we get real numbers.
Malik adds: And I could build a simple bat-and-ball game, so there is something easy for everyone to try.
Layla finishes: Then let's choose a time when no one has to miss out. Each idea made the last one better.

teacherSessions.title: Omar makes room for a quiet voice
lines: The team was talking quickly, and Dina had not said anything for a while.
Omar noticed and said: Dina, you are good at ideas. What do you think?
Dina suggested inviting the younger children too, which no one else had thought of.
Because Omar listened and encouraged her, the team ended up with a better plan.

teacherSessions.title: The team shares out the jobs by skill
lines: Writing the questionnaire went to Dina, who is good with words and ideas.
Asking children went to Omar, who is friendly and enjoys talking to people.
Recording the answers went to Grace, who is good with numbers and tables.
Building the game and the stall went to Malik, who likes making things by hand.
Keeping the plan and the time on track went to Layla, who is organised. Everyone had a fair share that matched their skill.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring your list of jobs and your idea of who could do each one.
As a group, agree together who takes which task, and check that the share feels fair to everyone.
This is real collaboration: you planned with your AI tutor, and now you decide together as a team.

teacherSessions.title: Grace and Malik find a middle way
lines: Malik wanted to spend the time building a game. Grace wanted to spend it running a simple race.
Instead of arguing, they listened to each other's reasons.
They found what they agreed on: both wanted something that every child could join.
They agreed a fair plan: a short race first, then Malik's game, each made a little smaller. The disagreement was resolved, and the team moved on happily.

teacherSessions.title: The team decides what to do first
lines: The team had three ideas: a sports afternoon, new posters, and asking for more balls.
They could only do one really well before the next teacher session, so they prioritised.
They asked: which is most important, most likely to get more children playing, and realistic in our time? Will we all stay happy doing it?
The sports afternoon won, because it would bring the most children in, and the whole team was keen to run it.

teacherSessions.title: Layla keeps the team on time
lines: Halfway through the session, Layla checked the schedule. The survey was taking longer than planned.
Instead of rushing, the team made a calm choice: finish the survey properly now, and move the poster to the next session.
Good time management is not about going faster. It is about noticing early and changing the plan together.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring an action plan you drafted with your AI tutor, with a step for each member.
As a group, agree the who and the by-when for each step, and set its starting colour.
Next time you meet, update the colours together and decide what to do about anything still Red.

teacherSessions.title: The team looks back honestly
lines: After the sports afternoon, the team evaluated their work.
About themselves: Grace felt she could have encouraged others more; Malik was proud he finished his game on time.
About the team: they agreed they shared the work fairly and reached their goal, but next time they will plan the time better.
Judging your work kindly and honestly is how a team gets better, project after project.

teacherSessions.title: The team's whole journey, from side-line to sports afternoon
lines: They agreed a shared outcome: more children take part in sport and play.
They shared ideas and built on them, and divided the jobs by skill.
They made a schedule with parallel work, and resolved a disagreement about the games.
They prioritised the sports afternoon, planned it in a What-When-Where-Who-Why table, and tracked it with Red, Amber and Green.
They ran the afternoon, more children joined in, and then they evaluated their teamwork honestly.

By following this cycle, five friends turned a worry about who gets to play into a real change at their school. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on your own team project, planning each step with your AI tutor and carrying it out with your group.

toolkit.title: The collaboration cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your team project, good collaboration follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Agree a shared outcome: the one result the whole team wants.
Share ideas: make suggestions and build on each other's.
Listen and encourage: hear everyone, especially the quiet voices.
Divide the tasks: fairly, and by each person's skill.
Schedule: who does what, how long, and when, using parallel work and dependencies.
Prioritise: choose the most important action if you cannot do everything.
Work positively: stay friendly, and resolve any disagreements fairly.
Track with a RAG action plan: Red, Amber and Green.
Evaluate: judge how well you and your team worked, and how to improve.

toolkit.title: The Collaboration skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Collaboration means working together with other people to reach a shared goal, called a shared outcome. It is not just being in the same room. A team is collaborating when they share one outcome, share out the work fairly, and help each other get there.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, share ideas and listen, so the team's thinking is better than any one person's. Second, work fairly and positively, so everyone feels useful and problems get solved kindly. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 6 Collaboration learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your collaboration skills grow in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for making and building on suggestions
toolkit.intro: Use these to add your own ideas, and to grow other people's ideas instead of blocking them.
items: I have an idea: we could ...
What if we tried ...?
Even better, we could ...
Building on that, what if we also ...?
Yes, and we could add ...
That gives me an idea: what about ...?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for listening and encouraging others
toolkit.intro: Use these to make sure everyone is heard, especially the quieter members of your team.
items: So you mean we could ...? (to show you listened)
That is a good start, tell us more.
You are good at this, what do you think?
I like that idea because ...
We have not heard from you yet, would you like to share?
Thank you, that really helps the team.

toolkit.title: Dividing tasks fairly, by skill
toolkit.intro: Share the jobs so that each one matches a person's skill, and everyone has a fair share. Copy this table to plan the division.

toolkit.title: A schedule grid: who, how long, when
toolkit.intro: Turn your tasks into a schedule. In the last column, show the order and the links: write First, or After task 2, or At the same time as task 3. Remember, parallel tasks happen together, and a dependency must wait for another task to finish.

toolkit.title: Managing your team's time
toolkit.intro: A plan only helps if the team keeps to it. Time management is not about hurrying; it is about noticing how the time is going and making calm choices together. Use these habits.
items: Agree at the start how long you have, and roughly how long each task should take.
Check the schedule partway through, not just at the end, so you spot a delay early.
If a task runs late, decide together what to move, shorten, or drop, rather than rushing everything.
Keep your eyes on the shared outcome, and spend your minutes on what matters most to reach it.
Give one member, like a timekeeper, the job of gently reminding the team of the clock.

toolkit.title: Prioritising: which action should we do first?
toolkit.intro:
When your team has more ideas than time, prioritise: choose the most important action to do first. Ask these checking questions about each possible action.

Then explain your choice using these starters: The action we are prioritising is ..., followed by Firstly ..., In addition ..., Furthermore ..., and Finally ...
items: Is it about an important problem that really needs action?
Will it actually change what people do?
Is the outcome realistic in the time and with the help we have?
Will the whole team stay in agreement and be happy doing it?
Do we need help from outside the team, and can we get it?

toolkit.title: Problem, action, outcome: a flowchart template
toolkit.intro: Read each row left to right: this shared problem, so we take this action together, to reach this shared outcome. The middle column is the part your team does.

toolkit.title: An action plan with Red, Amber and Green
toolkit.intro: Break your shared outcome into steps and track each one. Update the status colour every time your team meets.

toolkit.title: Resolving disagreements: a step-by-step guide
toolkit.intro:
Disagreements are normal. What matters is how you resolve them. Follow these four steps.

Keep your voice calm and friendly. Attack the problem, never the person. A disagreement resolved well often makes a team stronger than before.
items: Listen to each side, letting each person explain without being interrupted.
Find what you agree on, which is almost always the same shared outcome.
Suggest a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

toolkit.title: A good team member and a good team
toolkit.intro: Use these as a checklist for how to behave in a team.

toolkit.title: A good team member ...
items: always listens, does their fair share, and encourages others.
always shares ideas and builds on other people's.
never puts a teammate down or takes over every job.

toolkit.title: A good team ...
items: always agrees a shared outcome and divides the work fairly.
always manages its time and resolves disagreements kindly.
never leaves one person to do everything, or ignores a quiet voice.

toolkit.title: Making the most of your teacher sessions
toolkit.intro: Remember the pattern of this unit: plan and practise with your AI tutor, then do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions. Here is how to make each session count.
items: Come prepared: bring the plan, schedule or action plan you drafted with your AI tutor.
Start by agreeing your shared outcome, and what you want to finish in this session.
Share out the jobs quickly, using each person's skill, so no time is wasted.
Listen to everyone, and check the quieter members have had their say.
Near the end, update your action plan colours and agree who does what before next time.

activities.title: Choose your project and your shared outcome
activities.label: Activity 1: Choose your project and your shared outcome
activities.intro: Every team starts by agreeing what it is working towards. First choose a project, then write your shared outcome: the one result the whole team wants, in a single clear sentence. A good shared outcome is small enough for your team to reach, but big enough to be worth doing. If you are not sure, start with one of the ideas above and make it your own.
steps: Write the project you will work on: 'Our team project is ...'.
Write your shared outcome in one sentence: 'Our shared outcome is ...'.
Write one reason this matters, both to your team and to your school or community.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your project and your shared outcome sentence.
Ask it: is my shared outcome clear, and is it something a team of children could really reach?
Ask the tutor to help you make the sentence sharper and simpler.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Share your shared outcome with your group.
Together, agree on one shared outcome you all want, in a single sentence everyone could repeat.

activities.title: Make a suggestion, then build on others
activities.label: Activity 2: Make a suggestion, then build on others
activities.intro: Great teams grow one idea together instead of fighting for separate ones. Here you practise making a suggestion and building on other people's ideas. Building on an idea is almost always better than blocking it. When you say 'even better, we could ...', you keep the good part of a teammate's idea and add to it, so nobody feels their idea was thrown away.
steps: Write one suggestion for your project, starting with 'We could ...'.
Now build on it twice, as if you were a teammate: 'Even better, we could ...' and 'Building on that, what if we ...'.
Notice how the idea gets stronger each time you add to it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your first suggestion.
Take turns building on it: the tutor adds an idea, then you add to the tutor's idea, four times in all.
Ask the tutor which version of the idea is strongest, and why.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Try the same building-on game with your group. One person suggests; each person adds Even better, we could ...
See how much better the idea becomes once the whole team has built on it.

activities.title: List the tasks, then divide them fairly by skill
activities.label: Activity 3: List the tasks, then divide them fairly by skill
activities.intro: A shared outcome needs many jobs done. List them, then match each job to the skill it needs, so your team can divide the work fairly and by skill.
steps: List at least six tasks your project needs done.
Next to each task, write the skill it needs, such as drawing, planning, talking to people, or building.
Decide who in your team could do each one, and why.

activities.title: Build a schedule with parallel work and dependencies
activities.label: Activity 4: Build a schedule with parallel work and dependencies
activities.intro: Now turn your task list into a schedule: who does each task, how long it takes, and when it happens. Use two clever ideas to save time.
steps: Fill in the schedule table below for your project.
In the last column, write First, or After task 2, or At the same time as task 3, to show the order and the links.
Mark which tasks are parallel and which are dependencies.

boxes.title: Parallel work and dependencies
lines: Parallel tasks can be done at the same time by different people, so the team finishes sooner.
A dependency is a task that must wait until another one is finished first.
For each task, ask: can this run at the same time as another, or must it wait for something else?

boxes.title: A model note about order and links
lines: Agree the date — 10 minutes — First; everything depends on it.
Make posters — 25 minutes — At the same time as the survey (parallel work).
Record the answers — 20 minutes — After the survey (a dependency: it must wait).
Because two tasks run in parallel, the whole plan fits into less time than doing every job one after another.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your schedule to your AI tutor.
Ask it: which of my tasks could be done in parallel, to save time?
Ask the tutor which task must be done first, because other tasks depend on it.

activities.title: Fill a problem, action, outcome flowchart
activities.label: Activity 5: Fill a problem, action, outcome flowchart
activities.intro: A flowchart helps a team see how an action joins a problem to a result. Fill in three rows for your topic. Read each row left to right: this problem, so we do this, to reach this outcome.

boxes.title: A model row to copy
lines: Shared problem: some children never join in sport at break.
Action, working together: run a sports afternoon with easy games and invite every child.
Shared outcome: more children take part in sport and play.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three flowchart rows to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does each action really lead from the problem to the outcome?
Ask the tutor to help you improve any row where the action seems too small to reach the outcome.

activities.title: Prioritise which action to do first
activities.label: Activity 6: Prioritise which action to do first
activities.intro: Teams usually have more ideas than time. Practise prioritising: choosing the most important action to do first, and explaining why.
steps: List three possible actions your team could take.
For each one, answer the checking questions: is it important? will it change what people do? is it realistic? will the team stay happy? do we need outside help?
Choose one action, and justify it: 'The action we are prioritising is ... Firstly ... In addition ... Finally ...'.

boxes.title: A model justification
lines: The action we are prioritising is running a sports afternoon.
Firstly, it is the most likely to get more children playing, which is our shared outcome.
In addition, it is realistic: we can prepare it in two sessions.
Finally, the whole team is keen to do it, so we will stay in agreement.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your three possible actions.
Ask it to help you weigh each one against the checking questions.
Say your justification out loud, and ask the tutor if your reasons are strong and realistic.

activities.title: Plan your actions in a What, When, Where, Who, Why table
activities.label: Activity 7: Plan your actions in a What, When, Where, Who, Why table
activities.intro: Turn your chosen action into a clear plan by answering five questions about it. This changes a vague wish into something a team can really do.
steps: Write your team's shared outcome at the top of the table.
Fill in at least three actions, giving the What, When, Where, Who, and Why for each.
Check that every action names who does it and why it will help.

boxes.title: A model row
lines: What: put up posters inviting everyone to the sports afternoon.
When: this week. Where: the school entrance and every classroom.
Who: the creative members of the team design and put them up.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your action table to your AI tutor.
Ask it: is any action vague, and how could I make it clearer?
Ask the tutor to check that each action names a person and a reason.

activities.title: Practise resolving a disagreement
activities.label: Activity 8: Practise resolving a disagreement
activities.intro: Disagreements are a normal part of teamwork. Practising a calm way through them means you will be ready when a real one comes up.
steps: Think of a disagreement your team might have, such as which game to play or who does a popular job.
Write each side's reason fairly, as if you cared about both.
Write one thing both sides agree on, and one fair middle way.

boxes.title: Four steps to resolve a disagreement
lines: Listen to each side without interrupting.
Find what both sides agree on, usually the same shared outcome.
Suggest a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

boxes.title: A model resolved disagreement
lines: Side one wants a race; side two wants a ball game. Each explains why, and both listen.
What they agree on: both want a game that every child can join.
A fair middle way: a short race first, then the ball game, each made a little smaller.
Both sides are happy, and the team moves on. That is a disagreement resolved well.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe the disagreement to your AI tutor, and ask it to take the other side.
Practise the four steps out loud, all the way to agreeing a middle way.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I listen, stay calm, and treat the other side fairly?

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: If a real disagreement comes up in your group, use the same four steps.
Notice how much easier it is to sort out, now that you have practised.

activities.title: Build an action plan with Red, Amber and Green
activities.label: Activity 9: Build an action plan with Red, Amber and Green
activities.intro: Now pull your project together into an action plan you can track. Break your shared outcome into steps, and for each one write who does it, by when, and what is needed. Give each step a starting colour: Red for not started, Amber for started but not finished, and Green for complete.
steps: Fill in the action plan below with at least four steps.
Give every member of your team at least one step, so the work is shared.
Put the steps in a sensible order, with anything that must come first near the top.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your action plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are my steps in a sensible order, and is anything missing?
Ask the tutor what a team should do about a step that is still Red the day before its deadline.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Agree the action plan with your group, and give everyone a step.
Next time you meet, update the colours together and decide what to do about anything still Red.

activities.title: Encourage others and give kind, useful feedback
activities.label: Activity 10: Encourage others and give kind, useful feedback
activities.intro: A great teammate helps others feel good about their work. A simple, kind way to give feedback is two stars and a wish: two things a person did well, and one friendly suggestion. Kind feedback is not just being nice. When people feel their work is noticed, they try harder and share more ideas, and the whole team gets better.
steps: Think of a teammate you worked with, in your group or at home.
Write two stars: two things they did well.
Write one wish: one kind suggestion, starting with 'Next time, you could ...'.
Write one thing you did to encourage someone during the work.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two stars and a wish to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does my feedback sound kind and encouraging, not like a put-down?
Ask the tutor to help you reword the wish so it feels friendly and helpful.

boxes.title: A family touch
lines: Do a small job with someone at home, such as cooking or tidying, as a team.
Afterwards, give them two stars and a wish, and ask them to do the same for you.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does collaboration mean?
practice.answer: Collaboration means working together with other people to reach a shared goal. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: The one result a whole team is working towards is called the shared ______.
practice.answer: Outcome (the shared outcome).

practice.prompt: True or false: in a good team, only the leader is allowed to give ideas.
practice.answer: False. In a good team, everyone gives ideas, not only the leader.

practice.prompt: When a teammate makes a suggestion and you add to it to make it better, you are ______ on their suggestion.
practice.answer: Building (building on their suggestion).

practice.prompt: Name one thing you could say to encourage a quieter teammate to share their idea.
practice.answer: Any friendly invitation, such as: You are good at ideas, what do you think? or That is a good start, tell us more.

practice.prompt: When you share out the jobs, you should divide them ______ and by each person's ______.
practice.answer: Fairly; skill (divide the tasks fairly, by each person's skill).

practice.prompt: In a schedule, two tasks that can be done at the same time are called ______ tasks.
practice.answer: Parallel tasks.

practice.prompt: A task that cannot start until another task is finished is said to have a ______ on that task.
practice.answer: A dependency (it depends on the other task being finished first).

practice.prompt: When two teammates disagree, name one good thing to do first.
practice.answer: Listen to each side without interrupting. (Also correct: find what both sides agree on.)

practice.prompt: In a problem, action, outcome flowchart, what belongs in the middle column?
practice.answer: The action the team takes together to get from the problem to the outcome.

practice.prompt: Choosing the most important action to do first is called ______.
practice.answer: Prioritising.

practice.prompt: In an action plan, what does a Red status mean, and what does Green mean?
practice.answer: Red means the step has not started yet; Green means it is complete.

practice.prompt: Give one example of good time management in a team.
practice.answer: Any sensible example, such as: checking the schedule partway through, and moving a task that is running late instead of rushing.

practice.prompt: When you look back and judge honestly how well your team worked, you are ______ your teamwork.
practice.answer: Evaluating (also acceptable: reflecting on your teamwork).

practice.prompt: Name one thing a good team member always does.
practice.answer: Any one of: listens to others, encourages people, does their fair share, keeps to the plan, stays positive.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each collaboration word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Shared outcome
options: A. To share the tasks out between the team members.
B. The one result the whole team is working towards.
C. To decide which action is most important to do first.
D. The part you add to help your team, such as an idea or a job.
E. To judge honestly how well you or your team worked.
F. To sort out a disagreement fairly, so the team can move on.
practice.answer: B — The one result the whole team is working towards.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Contribution
practice.answer: D — The part you add to help your team, such as an idea or a job.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Prioritise
practice.answer: C — To decide which action is most important to do first.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Resolve
practice.answer: F — To sort out a disagreement fairly, so the team can move on.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Divide
practice.answer: A — To share the tasks out between the team members.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evaluate
practice.answer: E — To judge honestly how well you or your team worked.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Dina has a good idea but is too shy to say it, and the group is loud. What could Omar do to help?
practice.answer: Omar could listen and gently invite Dina in, for example by saying: Dina, you are good at ideas, what do you think? This encourages the quieter voice.

practice.prompt: Two teammates both want the fun job of building the game, and neither wants to record the answers. How could the team divide the work fairly?
practice.answer: They could divide by skill and take turns, so the fun jobs and the less popular jobs are shared, and each person does something that suits them.

practice.prompt: The team cannot make the posters until the date of the sports afternoon is decided. What is this link called, and which task should be scheduled first?
practice.answer: This link is a dependency. Deciding the date should be scheduled first, because the posters depend on it.

practice.prompt: Grace and Malik disagree about which game to play at the afternoon. What is a good first step to resolve it?
practice.answer: A good first step is to listen to both sides fairly, then find what they agree on, which is usually the same shared outcome.

practice.prompt: The day before the deadline, one step in the action plan is still Red. What should the team do?
practice.answer: The team should manage their time: help each other, make the step smaller if needed, or move a less important task, so the Red step gets done.

vocabulary.meaning: A list of the steps a team will take, saying who does each and by when.
Working together with other people to reach a shared outcome.
The part you add to help your team, such as an idea or a job you do.
A choice the team makes together.
A task that cannot start until another task is finished.
Times when team members do not agree; a normal part of teamwork.
To share the tasks out between the team members.
To help someone feel able to join in and share their ideas.
To judge honestly how well you or your team worked.
In a way that gives everyone a reasonable share.
Made better than it was before.
An important subject or problem that a team wants to solve.
The result the team reaches at the end.
Two or more tasks that can be done at the same time.
To decide which action is most important to do first.
Something that is not working well and needs solving.
Thinking carefully about how you and your team worked.
Sorted out or settled fairly, as when a disagreement is ended.
A plan of who does what, for how long, and when.
The one goal the whole team is working to reach.
The things a person is good at, such as drawing, planning or building.
A quick way to show if a task is not started, started, or complete.
People working together, each doing their part, to reach a shared goal.

mistakes: Starting the work before agreeing a clear shared outcome.
One person doing every job while the others watch.
Blocking ideas with a put-down instead of building on them.
Forgetting the quiet members, so their good ideas are never heard.
Making a plan but not watching the time, so the team runs out of it.
Letting a disagreement turn into a fight instead of resolving it fairly.
Finishing a project without evaluating how the team could do even better.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does collaboration mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Collaboration means working together with other people to reach a shared goal. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: The one result a whole team is working towards is called the shared ______.
True or false: in a good team, only the leader is allowed to give ideas.
questions.modelAnswer: False. In a good team, everyone gives ideas, not only the leader.

questions.prompt: When a teammate makes a suggestion and you add to it to make it better, you are ______ on their suggestion.
Name one thing you could say to encourage a quieter teammate to share their idea.
questions.modelAnswer: Any friendly invitation, such as: You are good at ideas, what do you think? or That is a good start, tell us more.

questions.prompt: When you share out the jobs, you should divide them ______ and by each person's ______.
questions.modelAnswer: Fairly; skill (divide the tasks fairly, by each person's skill).

questions.prompt: In a schedule, two tasks that can be done at the same time are called ______ tasks.
A task that cannot start until another task is finished is said to have a ______ on that task.
questions.modelAnswer: A dependency (it depends on the other task being finished first).

questions.prompt: When two teammates disagree, name one good thing to do first.
questions.modelAnswer: Listen to each side without interrupting. (Also correct: find what both sides agree on.)

questions.prompt: In a problem, action, outcome flowchart, what belongs in the middle column?
questions.modelAnswer: The action the team takes together to get from the problem to the outcome.

questions.prompt: Choosing the most important action to do first is called ______.
In an action plan, what does a Red status mean, and what does Green mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Red means the step has not started yet; Green means it is complete.

selfAssessment.statement: I can work with others to solve a problem.
I can help plan teamwork to reach a goal.
I can agree a clear shared outcome with my team.
I can make suggestions and build on other people's suggestions.
I can listen to others and encourage everyone to join in.
I can help divide the tasks fairly, by each person's skill.
I can make a schedule showing who does what, how long, and when.
I can help resolve a disagreement in a friendly way.
I can make a problem, action, outcome flowchart.
I can prioritise which action my team should do first.
I can introduce useful ideas and work positively.
I can help manage my team's time to reach the goal.
I can track our steps with Red, Amber and Green.
I can evaluate how well I and my team worked.
